description: Creative team from the greater DMV area.
summary:
Our team of families and kids took on “Abandoned but not Forgotten” by telling the story of one small machine that changed how we explore Mars: the Ingenuity helicopter. We started by learning about several pieces of NASA hardware left on Mars. Adults acted out each machine’s landing and biggest contribution, and the kids interviewed them. Then the kids voted to focus on Ingenuity. Using the Pixar Story Spine, they wrote, illustrated, and built a short film about its journey.

Our film introduces school-age space fans to Ingenuity and the science it made possible. It was the first aircraft to make a powered, controlled flight on another planet. It was built to fly five test flights, but it flew 72 times. It also scouted terrain ahead of the Perseverance rover before damage to its rotor blades ended its mission in 2024. Ingenuity isn’t junk sitting in the Martian dust. It proved that flight on other worlds is possible. A story made by kids, for kids, helps the next generation remember it and dream about what flies next.
details:
What it does and how it works
Our project is a short kid-made film that tells the story of NASA’s Ingenuity helicopter, from its landing on Mars with the Perseverance rover to its final flight. We built it through a two-day creative process. First, the adults read NASA mission material and acted out several pieces of hardware left on Mars, and the kids interviewed those “machines” about their landings and biggest discoveries. The kids then chose Ingenuity as their favorite. Working in small groups, they wrote stories using the Pixar Story Spine (“Once upon a time… Every day… Until one day…”), presented them, and dot-voted on the best moments. The adults merged those moments into one script and storyboard. Then the kids created the characters, props, and scenes, and we filmed it with still shots and video.

Benefits and intended impact
The film introduces school-age space fans to a piece of hardware most people have never heard of, and to the science it made possible. Ingenuity proved that powered, controlled flight works in Mars’s thin atmosphere. It flew 72 times when it was built for five, and it scouted terrain for Perseverance. Our goal is for young viewers to see retired space hardware as part of a story of discovery, not as junk. We also want them to imagine what might fly on other worlds next. Because the story was written by kids, it speaks to kids in their own language.

Tools, hardware, and software

  • NASA mission pages and images for Ingenuity and Perseverance (our fact source)
  • Printed research packets
  • Paper, markers, and craft materials for characters and scenery
  • Phone for filming
  • Video editing we used 11 labs
  • Claude and ChatGPT

How it’s creative
Instead of starting from facts on a screen, we started with role-play. Adults became the machines, which made the hardware feel like characters with personalities and histories. The Story Spine gave young kids a simple structure for building a real narrative. The kids designed and built the whole world of the film by hand.

Factors we considered

  • Accuracy vs. imagination: Real events (landing, first flight, number of flights, end of mission) are kept factual. Any fanciful parts are clearly framed as a dream or the future, so viewers can tell fact from fiction.
  • Privacy: We followed the challenge rules on minors, so no children’s faces, voices, or names appear in the film.
  • Mixed ages: Our team included young children, so we built in breaks, paired kids with adults, and kept each activity short and hands-on.
  • Time: With one weekend, we simplified the story to fewer characters and minimal scene changes so the kids could finish it themselves.
  • Length: We cut the story down to fit the 30-second demo limit.
